content: RAG retrieves relevant information from external knowledge sources and augments the model input before generation. This separates frequently changing factual knowledge from model weights. Fine-tuning modifies model behavior or parameters and is generally more suitable for behavior/style adaptation than frequent factual updates. Very large long-context prompts can increase cost and latency and introduce irrelevant context or lost-in-the-middle effects. Retrieval helps ground generation in selected external evidence.
common_misconceptions: Fine-tuning is required whenever documents change

content: Chunking balances retrieval precision with sufficient generation context. Large chunks may mix topics and reduce retrieval precision; very small chunks may omit necessary surrounding context. Overlap can reduce boundary information loss. Pre-chunking prepares chunks offline for fast retrieval, while query-time chunking provides flexibility at additional runtime cost. Semantic chunking uses semantic similarity or topic boundaries to keep related content together.

Embeddings represent text as numerical vectors in a learned space where semantically similar text should be closer. Retrieval compares query and document embeddings using similarity or distance measures such as cosine similarity or Euclidean distance. Query and indexed document embeddings must be compatible; changing the embedding model without rebuilding the index can severely degrade retrieval and generally requires re-embedding the corpus.
common_misconceptions: Embeddings store the original text verbatim
Any embedding model can query an index produced by another model

content: Dense retrieval captures semantic similarity, while sparse lexical retrieval such as BM25 is effective for exact terms, identifiers, acronyms, and rare names. Hybrid retrieval combines their complementary strengths. Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines ranked lists using rank positions rather than incompatible raw score scales. A two-stage pipeline can use efficient first-pass retrieval followed by a more expensive reranker on a smaller candidate set. Retrieval quality must be assessed together with context quality and downstream generation quality.
common_misconceptions: Vector search is always superior to keyword search
Higher recall always guarantees better answers

content: Prompt engineering focuses on instructions and phrasing, while context engineering manages which information enters the limited model context and how it is structured. Long contexts can suffer lost-in-the-middle behavior and, over long interactions, repetition or instruction drift. Systems can mitigate this by filtering, reranking, summarizing, compressing, prioritizing relevant context, and storing state outside the prompt when appropriate.
common_misconceptions: A larger context window removes the need for context selection
Prompt wording alone solves context-management problems

content: RAG evaluation should separate retrieval quality from generation quality so failures can be localized. Retrieval metrics include Recall@k, MRR, and MAP. Grounded evaluation datasets can be created from trusted source contexts by generating question-answer pairs and filtering them for groundedness, relevance, and stand-alone quality. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation should provide supporting evidence, explicit scoring criteria, and structured evidence-based outputs to improve consistency.
common_misconceptions: End-to-end correctness alone identifies the failing component
An LLM judge needs no rubric or evidence

content: Production RAG systems must manage authorization, freshness, latency, cost, and observability. Metadata filtering can restrict retrieval by tenant or ACL before unauthorized content becomes a candidate. Common failures include wrong chunks, poor ranking, and stale indexes; mitigations include hybrid retrieval, reranking, and synchronized reindexing. Performance and cost should be measured stage by stage across embedding, retrieval, fusion, reranking, context construction, and generation. Production architectures typically separate offline ingestion/index maintenance from online query processing.
common_misconceptions: Prompt instructions alone are sufficient for access control
Optimization should begin without measuring pipeline stages
